The Labour government has been accused of “capitulation” in its trade relations with China as Britain’s transition to net zero faces a number of security risks.

A new report, published shortly before President Trump’s momentous trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, has highlighted the UK’s dependence on China for net zero-related technology and potential vulnerabilities in supply chains.

Policy Exchange researchers found that China accounts for 91 per cent of the UK’s solar imports, plus 94 per cent of permanent magnets used in wind power and around 70 per cent of global battery production that is used in electric vehicles.

The think tank’s report, titled ‘The China Trap’, warned that the transition to net zero has “shifted…into the hands of a hostile state”, just as fears grow that the three world leaders are striking a deal to carve up regional power and put Britain’s national security under threat.

Following the meeting, Trump, Xi and Putin agreed that the United Nations should be reformed, fuel production should be increased, international courts should not “abuse their jurisdiction” and nuclear war “must not be fought”.

The historic meeting laid bare the shift in global powers in the midst of conflicts in Eastern Europe and the Middle East, plus a potential invasion of Taiwan.

New findings on the UK’s economic ties with China point to the risks facing critical sectors such as energy.

Responding to Policy Exchange’s report, shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat said that the government had overseen a policy of “capitulation”.

“We have bowed to the energy output of China, swapping carbon dependency in the Middle East for solar panels in the Middle Kingdom,” Tugendhat said.

Labour peer Maurice Glasman said it was “strategically vital that Britain uncouples itself from China if it is to be a sovereign, prosperous and secure nation”.

The report argued that China’s dominance in the clean energy market was a “tool of economic statecraft” given the country had imposed export controls while Royal Navy drone boats were reportedly transmitting data to Chinese internet addresses.

Britain’s £40bn automotive export industry also faced risks as a result of China’s control of key supplies, analysts added.

The Labour government’s stance on China depends on manifesto wording stating that the country should “co-operate where we can, compete where we need to, and challenge where we must”.

On Thursday morning, defence secretary Wes Streeting defended the government’s approach to China ahead of his Chinese counterpart Admiral Dong Jun’s trip to London on Thursday.

“Our security services have been open about the risks arising from cyberattacks, espionage and foreign interference,” Streeting wrote in The Times.

“But recognising the depth of these disagreements must not lead us to the dangerous conclusion that co-operation is impossible or undesirable.

“Climate change will not respect ideological boundaries. China is both the world’s largest emitter of greenhouse gases and its greatest producer of renewable energy technologies. No credible global response can succeed without its participation.”

analysis.tldr: If global green energy supply chains get disrupted by geopolitical tensions involving China, India's own massive transition to renewable energy could face cost hurdles and supply delays.
the_story: A new report by the Policy Exchange think tank warns that Britain is heavily dependent on China for green technologies, including 91 percent of its solar imports and 94 percent of permanent magnets for wind power.
The report calls China's dominance a tool of economic statecraft, pointing out that China has already imposed export controls.
British politicians criticized their government's approach, warning that swapping old carbon dependency for clean energy reliance on a hostile state puts national security at risk.

Meanwhile, British defense secretary Wes Streeting defended co-operating with China on climate change, noting that China is both the world's largest greenhouse gas emitter and biggest producer of renewable technologies.
analysis.what_happened: A British think tank report revealed that the UK relies almost entirely on China for green energy supplies like solar panels and electric vehicle batteries. This sparked political debate over whether relying on a single dominant country for clean energy creates severe national security and supply chain risks, especially as global superpowers maneuver for influence.
analysis.analogy: It is like relying on just one local grocery shop for all your daily food; if that shop owner decides to close or raise prices drastically, your household has nowhere else to quickly turn for dinner.
why_it_matters_india: India is also aggressively expanding its solar and electric vehicle sectors, heavily relying on imported components and raw materials from global markets.
If major economies like Britain and the US start fiercely competing with China or restricting trade for security reasons, global supply chains for clean tech can get congested or expensive.
Higher global prices for solar panels and batteries feed straight into India's domestic renewable energy installation costs.
This can squeeze profit margins for Indian green energy companies and potentially slow down the government's clean energy goals.

impacts.rationale: If clean energy equipment becomes globally scarce or expensive due to trade restrictions, building renewable power projects costs more, eventually raising electricity costs for everyone — generally bad for consumers.
Global trade conflicts and supply disruptions usually cause nervousness among big foreign investors (FIIs), leading to broader stock market dips which affect regular investors' portfolios.

impacts.target: Green energy and EV stocks in India
impacts.rationale: Higher import costs or disrupted component supplies can hurt the profitability of Indian renewable companies, which is bad for shareholders.

watch_next: New trade restrictions or export controls placed by China on raw materials and green technologies
How Indian renewable energy companies manage their raw material sourcing
analysis.caveats: The article focuses primarily on Britain's political debate, so any direct impact on India depends entirely on how global supply chains react to broader geopolitical shifts.

items.title: India's oil, gas import bill jumps 60% in Oct as Brent nearly doubles; cooking-gas usage falls
items.summary: Bill surges from $10 billion in October 2025 to $16 billion in October 2026

events.article_text:
Over April-October, the net import bill reached $97.7 billion, up from $70.3 billion a year earlier. Crude imports rose 2.7 per cent in volume but cost $111.0 billion, against $72.3 billion | Image: Bloomberg

India's net oil and gas import bill rose 60 per cent year-on-year to $16 billion in October as Brent crude averaged $124.77 a barrel, almost double that of a year earlier, according to data from the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC), part of the oil ministry.

The net bill was $10.0 billion in October 2025. Crude imports alone cost $19.5 billion, against $10.4 billion a year ago, even though volumes rose only 11 per cent to 23.3 million tonnes. LNG imports cost $1.3 billion, and petroleum product exports brought in $6.3 billion.

Brent averaged $116.77 in September and $64.75 in October 2025. The Indian basket averaged $119.91 in October, against $65.08 a year earlier.

Consumption of Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) fell 12.3 per cent in October and 15.1 per cent in April-October. The number of active domestic LPG customers stood at 32.6 crore on November 1, down from 33.4 crore on April 1, the PPAC data showed.

Direct private LPG imports fell 83.8 per cent in October and 97.3 per cent in April-October. Packed domestic LPG sales by state-run companies fell 11.8 per cent in October, and bulk LPG sales fell 49.1 per cent. Auto LPG sales rose 23.9 per cent.

Imports of petroleum products fell 41.2 per cent in October and 49.3 per cent in the fiscal year so far. PPAC attributed the fiscal-year decline mainly to lower imports of LPG, pet coke and fuel oil.

The International Energy Agency said in its World Energy Outlook 2026 that LPG imports fell by over 50 per cent in the first two months of shipping disruption through the Strait of Hormuz.

Other fuels held up better. Diesel consumption rose 12 per cent in October to 8.5 million tonnes, petrol rose 3.5 per cent, and bitumen rose 16.5 per cent. Total petroleum product consumption rose 2.7 per cent to 20.5 million tonnes in October. It was still down 3.2 per cent in April-October at 134.2 million tonnes.

Natural gas consumption fell 7.27 per cent to 5,707 million standard cubic metres in October. LNG imports fell 6.94 per cent to 3,014 million standard cubic metres.

India processed 24.1 million tonnes of crude in October, up 7.1 per cent, or about 5.70 million barrels a day. Of that, 22.0 million tonnes were imported crude, and domestic output was 2.1 million tonnes. Imports met 88.7 per cent of crude consumption in October.

Domestic crude and condensate output was 2.3 million tonnes. Import dependency for natural gas stood at 52.8 per cent in October.

Ethanol blending in petrol stood at 20 per cent in October, PPAC data showed.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

analysis.tldr: When global crude prices double, India's overall import bill swells, which can put pressure on the rupee and eventually make everyday fuel and imported goods costlier for everyone.
the_story: India's net oil and gas import bill rose 60 percent year-on-year to $16 billion in October, according to data from the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC).
Brent crude (the global benchmark price for oil) averaged $124.77 a barrel in October, almost double the price from a year earlier.
Crude imports cost $19.5 billion in October compared to $10.4 billion a year ago, even though physical volumes only rose 11 percent to 23.3 million tonnes.
Over the April-October period, the net import bill reached $97.7 billion, up from $70.3 billion a year earlier.
Consumption of Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG [cooking gas]) fell 12.3 percent in October, while direct private LPG imports dropped 83.8 percent.
analysis.what_happened: India's net oil and gas import bill jumped 60 percent to $16 billion in October. This happened because Brent crude prices nearly doubled to average $124.77 a barrel, making every barrel of imported oil much more expensive even though the actual amount of oil bought grew by a smaller margin.
analysis.analogy: It is like a household whose monthly grocery bill shoots up because the price of wheat and rice doubles overnight, forcing the family to spend a much larger share of their income just on basic survival.
why_it_matters_india: Global crude oil prices surge because of international market pressures.
India must buy more expensive oil from abroad, forcing the country to spend vastly more dollars.
Higher dollar outflows put depreciation pressure on the rupee (each rupee buys fewer dollars).
A weaker rupee and expensive oil make importing almost everything costlier, fueling overall inflation (rising prices for goods and services).

impacts.rationale: Buying costlier oil requires more dollars, which drains foreign exchange reserves and weakens the rupee — bad for importers and travellers.
More expensive energy raises transportation and manufacturing costs across the board, leading to higher prices for everyday goods — bad for consumers.
As raw crude oil costs surge, retail fuel prices face upward pressure — bad for motorists and commuters.

watch_next: Whether global Brent crude prices stay near $125 a barrel or drop
Official updates on retail fuel pricing and domestic inflation numbers in India
analysis.caveats: If global crude prices reverse course and fall sharply in the coming weeks, the pressure on India's import bill could ease quickly.

events.headline: The secretive salamanders of the Himalayas

items.title: The secretive salamanders of the Himalayas
items.summary: Species File: Exploring India’s biodiversity, one species at a time. Every monsoon in Darjeeling, the Himalayan salamander emerges from the forest floor to breed in small ponds known locally as pokhris. Males and females engage in a delicate courtship dance, after which fertilised eggs are laid on half-submerged vegetation. The larvae hatch into the water […]

events.article_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

Species File: Exploring India’s biodiversity, one species at a time.

Every monsoon in Darjeeling, the Himalayan salamander emerges from the forest floor to breed in small ponds known locally as pokhris. Males and females engage in a delicate courtship dance, after which fertilised eggs are laid on half-submerged vegetation. The larvae hatch into the water over the next two weeks, then develop lungs and adopt a terrestrial lifestyle. Once sexually mature, they return to their birth ponds to breed.

There are about 830 species of salamanders worldwide, predominantly found in North America, Europe, and Asia. India hosts only two species.

The Himalayan salamander (Tylototriton himalayanus), also called the Himalayan crocodile newt, is found in eastern Nepal, the Darjeeling Himalayas, and western Bhutan. It has a brown body with a blunt snout and rows of knobby warts along its back that may release toxins when disturbed. Adults are found near water bodies from roughly late April to early October. They spend the rest of the year on land, hiding under rocks or logs.

The Manipuri newt (Tylototriton zaimeng), also known as the Zaimeng newt, was described only in 2023. It has a broad head, a rounded snout and short limbs. Its brown skin carries orange-yellow markings on the head, back, and sides, and on the palms and soles. It is restricted to the Khongtheng mountain range, Manipur, where it was first found at Zaimeng lake and in surrounding mountain lakes and ponds.

The Himalayan salamander is classified as vulnerable in the IUCN Red List. The scientists who described the Manipuri newt have suggested the same category for it, citing its highly restricted range. Both species receive the highest legal protection under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.

Salamanders’ wetland habitats are shrinking rapidly, being drained for housing and tourism and polluted by wastewater. Roads cut across migration routes, resulting in accidental roadkill. Only a small fraction of the species’ current habitat lies within protected areas, while most of the remaining habitat occurs on private land and tea estates.

In a story published by Mongabay-India in April 2026, Barkha Subba, conservation scientist and 2026 Whitley Award winner, said: “Meeting a salamander feels like meeting a messenger from deep evolutionary time — a reminder of how long nature has endured and how quickly we can lose it.”

Read more about how the Himalayan salamander is losing its habitat, and the measures being taken for its conservation.

Banner image: A Himalayan crocodile newt. Image by John P. Clare via Flickr (CC BY-NC-ND 2.0).

Government schemes have sought to accelerate this transition by providing financial support for deep-sea fishing vessels. Yet the move into deeper waters has proved far more complicated than policy documents suggest. Across the coastal states of India, fishing communities […]

analysis.tldr: A report on endangered salamanders in the Himalayas highlights local habitat loss, which does not directly alter consumer prices, markets, or the wider Indian economy.
the_story: India hosts only two species of salamanders out of about 830 worldwide: the Himalayan salamander and the Manipuri newt.
The Himalayan salamander is found in eastern Nepal, the Darjeeling Himalayas, and western Bhutan, and breeds in small ponds during the monsoon.
The Manipuri newt was described only in 2023 and is restricted to the Khongtheng mountain range in Manipur.
Both species are classified as vulnerable and receive the highest legal protection under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.
Their wetland habitats are shrinking due to housing, tourism, wastewater pollution, and roads cutting across their migration routes.
analysis.what_happened: Mongabay India published a biodiversity report detailing the life cycle, locations, and conservation challenges of India's two salamander species. The article highlights that their wetland habitats are shrinking rapidly due to development, though the report focuses purely on wildlife conservation rather than economic or financial changes.
analysis.analogy: It is like discovering rare antique items in your house that need special protection, which changes how you manage your living space but has no impact on your monthly grocery budget.
why_it_matters_india: The article discusses regional biodiversity and environmental conservation in Darjeeling and Manipur.
There is no mechanism in this environmental report that alters national inflation, interest rates, or currency values.
Financial markets and corporate stocks do not react to wildlife status updates of regional amphibians.

analysis.caveats: This article is purely about wildlife conservation and contains no financial data or market-moving news.

items.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive on life support outside the body…

events.article_text:
Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive on life support outside the body for seven weeks, smashing the previous record of about two weeks.

They achieved the feat by connecting a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.

The approach could open up new possibilities in biomedical engineering, from repairing damaged organs to growing new ones. Some researchers are even exploring artificial wombs.

Take a closer look at the technology keeping human organs alive.

After a tough few years littered with high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US: Sila has signed a deal with battery maker Panasonic Energy to supply silicon-carbon anode material that could be worth more than $1 billion.

The agreement will help Sila scale production, potentially bringing smaller, lighter batteries to market. But it also reveals how battery politics have shifted. The factory is backed by a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department—and the industry is increasingly focused on geopolitics rather than the energy transition.

Find out what this deal reveals about the US battery industry.

events.headline: Make in India Surges : Exports soar across ASEAN , EU & Japan

items.title: Make in India Surges : Exports soar across ASEAN , EU & Japan

events.article_text:
Amid intensifying competition in international markets, India has recorded a notable achievement on the export front. In the first half of financial year 2026-27 (April-September), India’s exports expanded widely across its major free trade agreement (FTA) partners and the world’s large trading markets.

The growing reach of Indian products, from South-East Asia to Europe and East Asia, can be gauged from the fact that India’s exports to the ASEAN countries jumped 58 per cent to US$28.06 billion. Exports to partner countries of the South Asian Free Trade Area (SAFTA) rose by 22 per cent to $15.29 billion. Exports to the European Union also increased by five per cent to $38.79 billion.

Among the most outstanding features of India’s export performance are the double-digit gains in markets such as Singapore, Malaysia, Sri Lanka, Japan, South Korea and Oman. Exports to Singapore rose 103 per cent to $11.07 billion, while Malaysia recorded growth of 83 per cent and Sri Lanka 73 per cent. Exports to Oman also climbed 47 per cent to $3.29 billion. These figures indicate that India is building a strong presence not only in its traditional trading markets but also in new and fast-developing ones.

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) has emerged as the most important growth region in India’s export expansion. In April-September of financial year 2025-26, India’s exports to ASEAN countries stood at $17.75 billion; in the same period of 2026-27, they rose 58 per cent to $28.06 billion. Singapore and Malaysia played a particularly significant part in this growth.

India’s exports to Singapore grew from $5.45 billion to $11.07 billion, more than doubling in a single year. Demand for Indian products in the Malaysian market also surged: exports there rose 83 per cent, from $3.05 billion to $5.58 billion. Exports to Vietnam increased by 36 per cent to $3.83 billion, and to Indonesia by 36 per cent to $2.98 billion. Thailand, too, remained among India’s important export destinations, with exports of $2.65 billion.

The growing trade ties with ASEAN countries matter all the more because the region has become a vital hub of global manufacturing, electronics, energy, maritime trade and supply chains. The rising share of Indian exports in this market could create fresh opportunities for trade cooperation and industrial partnership in the future.

India’s neighbourhood has also seen a big leap, notably in Sri Lanka, a sign of strengthening trade relations with neighbouring countries. India’s exports to SAFTA partners rose 22 per cent to $15.29 billion, against $12.55 billion in the corresponding period of the previous financial year. Sri Lanka was among the fastest-growing markets.

Indian exports there rose 73 per cent, from $2.28 billion to $3.94 billion. Exports to Nepal grew 19 per cent to $4.37 billion, and to Bhutan 16 per cent to $711.4 million. The Maldives recorded a 52 per cent increase, with exports reaching $337.4 million. Bangladesh, with exports of $5.66 billion, remained India’s largest export destination in the SAFTA region.

Indian exports have also gained momentum in the developed industrial markets of East Asia. Exports to Japan rose 40 per cent to $4.10 billion, while exports to South Korea grew 24 per cent to $3.91 billion. The growing reach of Indian products in these two markets signals an expansion of India’s industrial and commercial ties.

Export growth in markets such as Japan and South Korea is significant because these countries are major centres of global technology, electronics, automobiles, machinery and advanced manufacturing. Wider business opportunities for Indian companies in these markets could help strengthen the country’s production capacity and international competitiveness.

The European Union remains one of India’s largest export markets. In the first half of 2026-27, India’s exports to the EU rose five per cent, from $36.97 billion to $38.79 billion. Markets such as Spain and Italy made a notable contribution to this growth.

Exports to Spain rose 45 per cent to $4.68 billion. In Italy, they grew 25 per cent to $4.55 billion. Exports to Germany increased 12 per cent to $6.34 billion, and to France nine per cent to $3.73 billion. Indian exports also recorded strong growth in comparatively smaller European markets such as Croatia, Bulgaria, Cyprus, Estonia and the Czech Republic.

Among the countries of the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), too, India’s exports rose by nearly five per cent to $1.03 billion. Exports to Switzerland grew 11 per cent to $758.4 million, and to Norway 14 per cent to $264 million. Liechtenstein recorded a 30 per cent increase.

Beyond Asia and Europe, India’s export ties have strengthened with other major trading partners as well. Exports to Oman rose 47 per cent to $3.29 billion. Exports to Australia grew 11 per cent to $4.10 billion, while those to the United Kingdom increased seven per cent to $7.32 billion. Mauritius, too, saw a remarkable 45 per cent rise.

The growth recorded across different geographical regions points to broad-based trade diversification. In global trade, building a presence across many countries and regions, rather than depending excessively on any single market, is important for economic stability. Rising exports simultaneously to ASEAN, South Asia, Europe, East Asia and West Asia are creating new opportunities for the Indian economy.

Thus, the first-half figures show that the scope of Indian exports is steadily widening and that the country’s trade relations are gaining strength in new geographical regions. This expansion provides an important foundation for making India a significant production and supply hub in global trade. It is certain that this progress of India as a nation gives all of us hope for a better future, alongside a stronger present.

analysis.tldr: Soaring exports mean more money flowing into Indian businesses, which generally helps strengthen the rupee and boosts local manufacturing sectors.
the_story: In the first half of financial year 2026-27 (April-September), India's exports expanded across major free trade agreement partners and global markets.
Exports to ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) countries jumped 58 per cent to US$28.06 billion, with Singapore doubling to $11.07 billion and Malaysia rising 83 per cent to $5.58 billion.
Exports to SAFTA (South Asian Free Trade Area) partner countries rose 22 per cent to $15.29 billion, led by a 73 per cent surge in Sri Lanka to $3.94 billion.
Exports to the European Union increased by 5 per cent to $38.79 billion, driven by strong gains in countries like Spain (up 45 per cent) and Italy (up 25 per cent).
East Asian markets also saw growth, with exports to Japan rising 40 per cent to $4.10 billion and South Korea growing 24 per cent to $3.91 billion.
analysis.what_happened: India's overseas sales grew significantly across multiple regions including Southeast Asia, Europe, South Asia, and East Asia during the first half of financial year 2026-27. This broad-based growth reflects higher international demand for Indian goods and stronger commercial ties through free trade agreements.
analysis.analogy: It is like a local shopkeeper who used to sell only in their own lane suddenly opening successful stalls across the whole city, bringing in much more cash.
why_it_matters_india: Indian companies sell more goods abroad -> bringing in more foreign currency
Higher foreign earnings -> strengthen the rupee (each rupee buys more dollars)
Stronger export demand -> creates more jobs and production in Indian manufacturing hubs
Broad trade partnerships -> protect the Indian economy from depending too heavily on any single country

impacts.rationale: More foreign money coming in from higher exports helps support the rupee, which is good for lowering import bills like crude oil.
Stronger international sales and manufacturing growth improve profit outlooks for Indian companies, generally boosting investor confidence.

watch_next: Full-year export data for the remainder of financial year 2026-27
Updates on trade agreements with key regions like ASEAN and the European Union
analysis.caveats: Global demand could slow down if international economic growth cools off in the coming months.

history.title: The day the dollar stopped being gold
history.what: President Nixon went on television on a Sunday evening and announced that the United States would no longer convert dollars into gold for foreign governments. The system that had governed world money since 1944 ended in a fifteen-minute broadcast, and it was never restored.
history.why: Under the Bretton Woods agreement every currency was pegged to the dollar and the dollar was pegged to gold at $35 an ounce. That worked only while America held enough gold to honour the promise. Spending on the Vietnam war and on domestic programmes meant far more dollars circulating abroad than America had gold to back. France and Britain began asking for the gold. The promise was arithmetically impossible to keep, and everyone could see it.
history.impact: Currencies began floating against each other for the first time in modern history, which is why exchange rates move every day now. The dollar fell about a third against major currencies over two years. Gold, freed from its fixed price, went from $35 to $850 by 1980. Inflation across the rich world moved into double digits, because the external discipline that had capped money creation was simply gone.
history.policy: The immediate response was wage and price controls — which failed within two years. The durable answer took another decade: central banks were made independent of elected governments and given an explicit inflation target, so that the discipline gold had imposed from outside was rebuilt inside the institutions instead.
history.consequence: We live in that world now. Money is a promise backed by an institution's credibility rather than by metal, which is precisely why central bank independence is defended so fiercely and why any political interference with a central bank frightens markets so much. It also made currencies a permanent variable in every cross-border investment — the reason a rupee investor has to think about the dollar at all.
history.pattern: When a fixed promise becomes arithmetically impossible, it does not get renegotiated gradually. It gets abandoned suddenly, usually on a weekend, and the people who prepared for the possibility do far better than the ones who trusted the promise because it had always held.
history.india_echo: India's own version came twenty years later, in 1991, for the same underlying reason: a promise the reserves could not fund. Today the echo is quieter but constant — the rupee's long slide against the dollar is the background weather of every Indian portfolio, and it exists because 1971 made currencies float.
history.watch_for: Any peg or price cap that requires ever-larger reserves to defend. Currency pegs, fuel price freezes, and support levels that "will always hold" all end the same way.
